text:
“Mama, we did it!”

Her mother cried as she held her daughter.

“Yes, my child. We did it.”

While other graduates celebrated with expensive gifts and parties, Nadia and her mother returned home to eat a modest meal of rice and stew.

But for them, that meal tasted better than any expensive dinner in the world.

They had survived.

And their story was only beginning.

After graduation, Nadia applied for dozens of jobs.

She attended interviews, submitted applications, and waited for phone calls that never came.

Eventually, she secured a job as an assistant at a small clothing company.

Her salary was modest, but she was grateful.

Nadia worked harder than everyone else. She arrived early, stayed late, and studied everything she could about the business.

She noticed that the company wasted money on poor marketing and failed to understand what customers wanted.

One evening, she prepared a detailed proposal showing how the company could attract more customers through affordable clothing, better designs, and online advertising.

She presented it to her manager.

He glanced at the document and laughed.

“Who asked you to teach us how to run a business?”

“I only wanted to help the company grow, sir.”

“Then concentrate on your job. You are an assistant, not a business expert.”

He threw the proposal onto his desk.

Nadia picked it up and walked away.

That night, she cried again.

But this time, she did not cry because someone had insulted her. She cried because she had finally realized that some people would rather watch you remain small than admit that you have something valuable to offer.

Instead of giving up on her idea, Nadia started researching the clothing industry in her spare time.

She saved a portion of every salary she received.

She learned about fabrics, suppliers, customer service, branding, and online sales.

After three years, she had saved enough money to rent a tiny shop.

She resigned from her job and opened a small clothing business.

Her mother was frightened.

“Nadia, what if this business fails? We don’t have money to start again.”

Nadia held her mother’s hands.

“Mama, I would rather try and fail than spend the rest of my life wondering what could have happened if I had tried.”

Her mother eventually gave her blessing.

Nadia named the business Nadia Styles.

At first, customers barely entered the shop.

Some days, she sold nothing.

She sat alone, staring at the clothes hanging on the racks, wondering whether she had made a terrible mistake.

But she refused to close the shop.

She began posting pictures of her designs online. She offered affordable prices, treated every customer with respect, and made sure every order was delivered properly.

Slowly, things began to change.

One customer recommended her to another.

A popular fashion influencer purchased one of her outfits and posted it online.

Within days, Nadia received more orders than she could handle.

She hired two workers.

Then five.

Then ten.

Within two years, her little shop became a recognized clothing brand.

She opened branches in other cities and eventually began supplying clothing to major retailers….

🟧 SNF PULSE — WASHINGTON JUST CHANGED THE ENERGY SANCTIONS CALCULATION.

While oil markets confront escalating Middle East supply risks, the White House has made a consequential policy decision.

President Trump signed an executive order waiving key provisions of the new Russia sanctions law before additional penalties were scheduled to take effect October 18.

The waived measures include proposed 100% tariffs targeting certain major purchasers of Russian oil and gas.

Existing Russia sanctions remain in place.

🟨 THE STORY ISN'T JUST RUSSIA.

It's the growing conflict between geopolitical pressure and energy affordability.

Washington is attempting to manage two competing objectives:

Maintain economic pressure on Russia while preventing additional disruptions to global energy supply.

The waiver reduces the immediate threat of another sanctions-driven trade shock.

But it doesn't resolve the underlying energy crisis.

🟨 WHAT THE MARKET IS PRICING IN

Oil markets are already confronting security threats across the Middle East, pressure on shipping routes and increasingly complicated supply relationships.

Additional restrictions on Russian energy could have introduced another layer of uncertainty.

The waiver changes that calculation.

The important distinction: avoiding new penalties is not the same as delivering additional physical supply.

Energy markets still need evidence that available barrels can reach buyers efficiently.

🟨 WHAT SNF IS WATCHING

Whether Russian energy exports increase measurably.

How major importing countries respond to the waiver.

Whether refined-product availability improves.

And whether any improvement in energy supply begins reducing inflation expectations and pressure on global bond markets.

SNF LENS

🟠 Signal: Washington waives new Russia-related sanctions and tariffs before implementation.

⚪ Noise: Assuming the decision immediately lowers oil prices or eliminates existing restrictions.

🟢 Confirmation: Observable export flows, improved product availability and reduced energy-market stress.

🔴 Risk: Further Middle East disruptions overwhelm the relief offered by the sanctions waiver.

🟨 THE BOTTOM LINE

Energy policy is becoming an increasingly important instrument of macroeconomic stabilization.

But sanctions relief cannot replace physical supply.

The market must now determine whether Washington's policy adjustment translates into actual energy availability, or simply removes one additional source of uncertainty.

For the Fed, the bond market and global equities, that distinction matters.

text:
Estados Unidos ofrece otros 17 millones de barriles de reservas estratégicas de petróleo a medida que se agrava la crisis del combustible.
Por Julianne Geiger - 16 de octubre de 2026, 13:30 CDT

Estados Unidos pondrá a la venta otros 17 millones de barriles de crudo de la Reserva Estratégica de Petróleo, un día después de que la AIE acelerara la liberación de reservas de emergencia, mientras los gobiernos se apresuran a introducir más petróleo y combustible en un mercado saturado.

El Departamento de Energía emitió el viernes una solicitud de propuestas para un intercambio de hasta 17 millones de barriles, parte de los 172 millones de barriles que Washington se comprometió a poner a disposición en virtud de la medida de emergencia de 400 millones de barriles anunciada en marzo por la AIE.

Actualmente, la Reserva Estratégica de Petróleo (SPR, por sus siglas en inglés) cuenta con unos 283 millones de barriles. Si las empresas extraen los 17 millones de barriles completos antes de que se realicen los reembolsos, las existencias se reducirían a aproximadamente 266 millones de barriles, lo que se sitúa justo dentro del rango de 250 a 300 millones de barriles que generalmente se considera la zona mínima operativa de la reserva.

Hay un inconveniente bastante importante: alguien tiene que querer el petróleo.

El Departamento de Energía ofreció en junio la última parte de su compromiso de marzo, exigiendo a las empresas que devolvieran el crudo prestado posteriormente con primas de hasta el 24%. Las empresas acordaron aceptar solo unos 500.000 barriles.

El gobierno lo está intentando de nuevo. El API estimó que las reservas de crudo de EE. UU. cayeron 11,12 millones de barriles la semana pasada, tras un descenso de 2,09 millones de barriles la semana anterior. Los inventarios comerciales han perdido más de 51 millones de barriles en las últimas 26 semanas.

La solicitud del viernes se produce tras una nueva escalada en la campaña de reservas de emergencia. La AIE anunció el jueves que sus miembros acelerarían la entrega de los aproximadamente 100 millones de barriles pendientes desde marzo, incluidos más de 20 millones de barriles de diésel, lo antes posible.

Washington está ofreciendo ahora 17 millones de barriles más, con una reserva estratégica de reservas (SPR) de 283 millones de barriles en un mercado que ya demostró este verano que endeudarse con el gobierno para obtener crudo con condiciones de pago costosas no es necesariamente un acuerdo que las refinerías deseen.

text:
I want to thank Marc Gendron for important message in the Post-Star. A candidate refusing to debate is like an applicant refusing to show up to a job interview: it's disqualifying, and raises more questions than it answers. 
---
Why I’m voting for Constantino
If you want a job, you show up for the interview. That's true for a line cook, a welder, or a schoolteacher, and it should be true for anyone asking to represent us in Congress.

Anthony Constantino understands that: that’s why he accepted all six dates offered by CBS6 for the debate, which was broadcast to every member of our communities. He was willing to stand in front of voters, take tough questions, and defend his record and his ideas in the open.
Blake Gendebien accepted none. Not one. The man asking us to trust him with a seat in Congress wouldn't spend a single evening answering questions alongside his opponent. What exactly was he afraid of?
Whatever the reason, the result is the same. Upstate voters are being asked to hire someone who refused to sit for the interview.

In a district as large as ours, stretching across hundreds of miles of small towns and rural roads, many voters will never meet the candidates in person. A televised debate is one of the only chances we get to see them side-by-side and judge for ourselves. By dodging every one, Gendebien told us he'd rather run on ads and talking points than face scrutiny. 

A congressman's whole job is to speak up for us when it's hard, to argue our case in rooms full of people who disagree. If Gendebien wouldn't defend himself in front of his own future constituents, how can we expect him to stand up for us in Washington?

Constantino was ready to make his case. Gendebien was hiding from his.
That’s why I’m voting for Anthony Constantino.

Marc Gendron
Plattsburgh

text:
AMERICA WAS ONCE THE LEADER OF THE FREE WORLD. WHAT HAPPENED?

Not long ago, the United States was the undisputed leader of the democratic world, a defender of international law, and a country whose promises carried enormous weight. American leadership inspired confidence among allies and forced aggressors to consider the consequences of their actions.

That began to change in 2014, when Russia invaded Ukraine and illegally annexed Crimea. President Barack Obama responded with sanctions and diplomatic pressure, but Washington failed to stop Russian aggression. This was particularly troubling because the United States had signed the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, providing security assurances to Ukraine in exchange for surrendering its nuclear arsenal.

The United Nations also demonstrated its weakness. With Russia holding veto power in the Security Council, the organization proved incapable of enforcing international law against a permanent member.

Compare this with Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990. The United States assembled an international coalition, defeated the aggressor, and restored Kuwait's sovereignty. American leadership was decisive. When Ukraine faced Russian aggression, however, Washington chose a fundamentally different approach.

Following Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, President Joe Biden initially acted with extreme caution. Washington offered Volodymyr Zelenskyy assistance with evacuation, but Ukraine's president refused to leave his country.

American military assistance eventually became essential to Ukraine's survival. Yet the Biden administration repeatedly delayed weapons deliveries, restricted their use, and appeared more concerned about Russian escalation than Ukrainian victory. In my opinion, Washington provided enough assistance to prevent Ukraine's defeat, but not enough to ensure Russia's defeat.

Instead of delivering peace, Trump became involved in another major conflict, this time with Iran, contributing to instability in the Persian Gulf, rising energy prices, and growing international economic uncertainty.

And somehow, Trump increasingly directs his anger toward Ukraine and President Zelenskyy rather than Vladimir Putin, the man responsible for invading Ukraine.

Meanwhile, America's relationships with its closest allies have deteriorated. Canada and the European Union, partners that stood beside Washington for generations, now face an American administration that frequently treats them more like competitors than friends.

Trump's approach to Russia is even more disturbing. His statements and decisions repeatedly raise questions about whether Washington still recognizes the fundamental difference between an aggressor and a country fighting for its survival.

How can Trump promise to make America great again while undermining the very alliances and international institutions that helped establish American greatness?

But blaming Trump alone would be unfair.

America's declining international credibility did not begin with his presidency. Under Obama, Biden, and Trump, Washington repeatedly demonstrated a growing unwillingness to match its declarations about democracy and international law with decisive action.

The consequences have accumulated over more than a decade.

For generations, America's greatest strength was never simply its military power, nuclear arsenal, or economic influence. It was the belief that the United States stood for something greater: freedom, democracy, sovereignty, and a rules-based international order.

That belief has been seriously damaged.

Nobody knows exactly what awaits America or the rest of the world. But I am convinced of one thing: the United States will never simply return to the international position it once occupied.

The world has fundamentally changed. Traditional alliances are being tested, global power is shifting, and humanity is approaching a period of profound political, economic, and social transformation.

text:
On the temporary prohibition question, I think we already have it. Chapter 27 lets a court order involuntary hospitalization for substance use disorder after an examination and a hearing with counsel, on a finding that the person has "lost the power of self-control" — nearly the words of an 1874 Connecticut statute. Anyone committed that way is already disarmed by subdivision (4). That's the drinker the history reaches, and he gets a hearing first. Subdivision (2) reaches a much larger group with no hearing at all.

On renunciation, the loyalist laws are the best analogue anyone has offered, and I think they fail on one detail. Those were wartime measures aimed at people who refused an oath they remained free to take at any time. Section 922(g)(7) offers no oath and no way back.

I've got a longer piece on this coming. Would value your eyes on it first if you're willing. It’s for my Greenbrier Street Brief Substack which goes to various West Virginia policymakers.
